relations.subject: server:failover
relations.evidence: Nodes can be either hard failed over or gracefully failed over.

relations.subject: server:failover
relations.evidence: Nodes can be either hard failed over or gracefully failed over.

relations.subject: server:hard-failover
relations.evidence: A hard failover means that the failover happens immediately but risks potential data loss. Graceful failover ensures that replication is up to date before the node is failed over so that there is no data loss, but the failover is not immediate.

relations.subject: server:hard-failover
relations.evidence: Note that if a node is already down, you must perform a hard failover.

relations.subject: server:cluster-quorum
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - stretched slightly from REST/statement gating to a CLI operation gate, since no closer predicate exists for 'this many participants must agree before the operation can proceed'
relations.evidence: In order to perform a failover, the cluster needs a quorum of nodes.

relations.subject: server:hard-failover
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - for the --force override that lets a hard failover proceed without quorum
relations.evidence: There are cases where the majority of nodes are unavailable, and it will be impossible to get a quorum. In those cases, this flag can be used to force a hard failover.

relations.subject: server:graceful-failover
relations.evidence: Note that a rebalance only occurs for graceful failovers (e.g., non-forced failovers).

notable_absence.finding: Failover is arguably the single most destructive manual operation in this batch - --hard --force can be forced through even without cluster quorum - yet, as with every other file in this batch, no specific RBAC role or privilege is ever named as required to invoke it. Only the generic 'unauthorized error' boilerplate appears.

cross_component_finding: This page is the direct primary source for a fact the promoted registry currently states only as a compressed parenthetical on server:hard-failover ('refused by default but overridable with CLI's --force + --hard'): the actual mechanism (a quorum requirement, refused by default, overridable only by combining --force with --hard) is spelled out here in full prose. Terminology matches the registry cleanly - 'hard failover' and 'graceful failover' are used identically to their promoted definitions, with no drift. Unlike the rebalance/rebalance-status/rebalance-stop trio, this page has substantive, non-boilerplate DESCRIPTION and OPTIONS prose (the quorum/--force mechanism), so the lighter-TW-review hypothesis shows up here less as terseness and more as a mechanism only ever documented in one place with no cross-link to the promoted registry's own compressed summary of it.
cross_product_finding: Not addressed on this page - no comparison to Capella's own failover handling (which is largely automated/managed) is made.
